summary: A local-technology feature follows Bob Anderson, a third-generation Illinois farmer who moved from skepticism to adopting smart farming after visiting the AgriTech Expo. Using an FMIS, soil sensors, precision irrigation, drones and data analytics with Claire Thompson, he cut water and pesticide use and raised yields. He also became a community leader, hosting workshops that spread precision agriculture among neighboring farmers.
one_line: Illinois farmer Bob Anderson adopts sensors, drones and analytics, cutting water and pesticide use, raising yields and inspiring his farming community.
key_facts: Bob Anderson is a third-generation farmer from Springfield, Illinois, who initially saw his smartphone only as a communication tool.
Bob Anderson was introduced to precision agriculture at the AgriTech Expo on October 3, 2023.
At the expo he saw drones for monitoring crop health, real-time soil sensors for moisture and nutrients, and data analytics platforms for optimizing planting and irrigation.
Bob began his smart farming experiment in spring 2024 with a grant from the Local Innovations in Farming initiative.
The first step was adopting a Field Management Information System (FMIS), which let Bob monitor every acre in detail.
Soil sensor data showed that not all of Bob's land needed the same amount of water, leading him to switch to precision irrigation.
Precision irrigation reduced Bob's water consumption by 20% in the first year while improving crop yield.
Drones provided high-resolution images that identified pest infestations and plant diseases before they were visible to the naked eye.
Using drones, Bob limited chemical applications to affected areas, and his pesticide use dropped by 35%.
Data scientist Claire Thompson, who specializes in agricultural analytics, helped Bob interpret his data and choose crop varieties suited to his soil.
The targeted cultivation of new crop varieties led to a 15% increase in Bob's yields.
Bob hosted community workshops that demystified technology and encouraged other farmers to explore precision agriculture.
Aquifer levels in the region were a growing concern, so water savings had a significant environmental impact.
